newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIUM'S COCKERILL SAMBRE H1 96 SEEN IN THE RED.
newsitem.headline: BELGIUM'S COCKERILL SAMBRE H1 96 SEEN IN THE RED.

text.p: Belgian steel maker Cockerill Sambre SA looks set to slide into the red when it announces half year 1996 results on Thursday, but analysts were divided over whether or not to recommend the share.
"In flat steel there is an improvement in volumes but not yet in prices," said Mignon, Hanart, Declerck analyst Isabelle Defranne.

Cockerill chairman Jean Gandois warned in April weak economic growth in neighbouring countries and lower orders would probably lead to a first half 1996 loss. In first half 1995 Cockerill made a group net profit of 3.1 billion francs.

Gandois has also predicted break-even or a loss for the full year, mainly due to losses at German car components unit Ymos and at Belgian unit Cockerill Mechanical Industries (CMI). Cockerill's 1995 group net profit was 3.2 billion francs.
Ymos has already announced a first half 1996 group pre-tax loss of 18.9 million marks versus a 10.3 million profit in the year ago period. It blamed the drop on its domestic business.

Banque Bruxelles Lambert analyst Olivier Heuschling forecast a first half current group loss of 600 million francs for Cockerill Sambre, adding he did not expect exceptional items to be "very dramatic".
However he considered the share a "buy".
"We have a target price of 190 francs in 12 months, based on a price to cashflow for 1997," he said. He calculated a price to cashflow of 3.5.
Cockerill shares closed at 133 francs on the Brussels bourse on Tuesday.
In an overall down channel since reaching 215 at the end of August 1994, the stock hit a 16-month low of 127 in July this year. Since then it has been caught in a range between 131 and 137 francs.

Kredietbank said it had a slightly negative rating on the stock. "Steel prices haven't reacted to the general economic pick up, and when they do, the price rise might not be as big as expected," one analyst at the bank said.

Mignon's Defranne said while she expected the steel industry to do better in coming months, she prefered Luxembourg steel stock Arbed over Cockerill because of the former's restructuring plan and its switch to electric furnaces.
However in the very short term, she noted Cockerill shares still had room to benefit from a heavier reweighting in the Bel-20 index of leading Belgian shares on September 20.
